A '''secure signature creation device''' ('''SSCD''') is a specific type of computer hardware or software that is used in creating an [[electronic signature]]. To be put into service as a secure signature creation device, the device must meet the rigorous requirements laid out under Annex II of [[eIDAS|Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (eIDAS)]], where it is referred to as a [[qualified electronic signature|qualified (electronic) signature]] creation device (QSCD). Using secure signature creation devices helps in facilitating online [[business processes]] that save time and money with transactions made within the [[Public sector|public]] and [[private sector]]s.<ref name="Turner-SSCD">{{cite web|last1=Turner|first1=Dawn M.|title=What is a secure signature creation device|url=https://www.cryptomathic.com/news-events/blog/secure-signature-creation-device|publisher=Cryptomathic|accessdate=18 November 2016}}</ref><ref name="Tuner_Understanding eIDAS">{{cite web|last1=Turner|first1=Dawn|title=Understanding eIDAS|url=https://www.cryptomathic.com/news-events/blog/understanding-eidas|publisher=Cryptomathic|accessdate=12 April 2016}}</ref>
<ref name="eIDAS-EUR-Lex">{{cite web|title=Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 23 July 2014 on electronic identification and trust services for electronic transactions in the internal market and repealing Directive 1999/93/EC|url=http://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=uriserv:OJ.L_.2014.257.01.0073.01.ENG|website=EUR-Lex|publisher=The European Parliament and the Council of the European Union|accessdate=18 March 2016}}</ref>

==Description==
The minimum requirements that must be met to elevate an electronic signature creation device to the level of a secure signature creation device are provided in Annex II of eIDAS. Through appropriate procedural and technical means, the device must reasonably assure the confidentiality of the data used to create an electronic signature. It further must ensure that the data used to create an electronic signature is unique and only used once. Lastly it shall only allow a [[Trust service provider|qualified trust service provider]] or [[certificate authority]] to create or manage a signatory’s [[electronic signature]] data.<ref name="Tuner_Understanding eIDAS" />

To ensure security, signature creation data used by the SSCD to create an electronic signature must provide reasonable protection through current technology to prevent forgery or duplication of the signature. The creation data must remain under the sole control of its [[Signature|signatory]] to prevent unauthorized use. The SSCD itself is prohibited from altering the signature’s accompanying data.<ref name="Turner-SSCD" />

When a trust service provider or certificate authority places an SSCD into service, they must securely prepare the device according to Annex II of eIDAS in fully compliance to the following three conditions:<ref name="ETSI-SSCD">{{cite web|title=Electronic Signatures and Infrastructures: Policy requirements for certification authorities issuing qualified certificates|url=https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/101400_101499/101456/01.04.03_60/ts_101456v010403p.pdf|publisher=European Telecommunications Standards Institute|accessdate=18 November 2016}}</ref><ref name="Turner-SSCD" />
# While in use or in storage, the SSCD must remain secure.
# Further, a reactivation and deactivation of the SSCD must occur under secure conditions.
# Any user activation data, include [[Personal identification number|PIN codes]] be delivered separately from the SSCD after being prepared securely.

==International security assurance requirements for SSCDs==

The secure signature creation device must also meet the international standard for [[computer security]] certification, referred to as the [[Common Criteria|Common Criteria for Information Technology Security Evaluation]] (ISO/IEC 15408).<ref name="ISO15408">{{cite web|title=ISO/IEC 15408-1:2009 Information technology -- Security techniques -- Evaluation criteria for IT security -- Part 1: Introduction and general model|url=http://www.iso.org/iso/catalogue_detail.htm?csnumber=50341|publisher=International Organization for Standardization (ISO)|accessdate=18 November 2016}}</ref> This standard gives computer system users the ability to specify security requirements via Protection Profiles (PPs) for security functional requirements (SFRs) and security assurance requirements (SARs).<ref name="Turner-SSCD" /><ref name="eIDAS-EUR-Lex" /> The trust service provider or certificate authority is the required to implement the specified requirements and attest to their product’s security attributes. A third-party testing laboratory then evaluates the device to ensure that the level of security is as claimed by the provider.<ref name="Turner-TrustServiceProviders">{{cite web|last1=Turner|first1=Dawn M.|title=Trust service providers according to eIDAS|url=https://www.cryptomathic.com/news-events/blog/trust-service-providers-according-to-eidas|publisher=Cryptomathic|accessdate=18 November 2016}}</ref>

==Central authentication service==

When a secure signature creation device is used as part of a [[Central Authentication Service|central authentication service]] (CAS), it may act as a CAS server in multi-tier authentication scenarios. The CAS software protocol allows users to be authenticated when signing into a [[web application]].

The common scheme for a CAS protocol includes the client’s web browser, an application requesting authentication and the CAS server. When authentication is needed, the application will send a request to the CAS server. The server will then compare the user’s credentials against its database. If the information matches, the CAS will respond that the user has been authenticated.<ref name="Turner-SSCD" /><ref name="eIDAS-EUR-Lex" />

==Legal implications regarding secure signature creation devices==

eIDAS has provided a tiered approach to determining the legal implications of electronic signatures. A signature that has been created with a secure signature creation device is considered to have the strongest [[Relevance (law)|probative value]]. A document or message that has been signed with such a device is [[non-repudiation|non-repudiable]], meaning the signatory cannot deny they are responsible for the creation of the signature.<ref name="Tuner_Understanding eIDAS" />

Regulation (EU) No 910/2014 (eIDAS) evolved from Directive 1999/93/EC, the [[Electronic Signatures Directive]]. The intent of the directive was to make [[EU Member State]]s responsible for creating legislation that would allow for the creation of the European Union’s electronic signing system. The eIDAS [[Regulation (European Union)|Regulation]] required all Member States to follow its specifications for electronic signatures by its effective date of 1 July 2016.<ref name="Turner-eIDAS-from-directive-to-reg">{{cite web|last1=Turner|first1=Dawn M.|title=eIDAS from Directive to Regulation - Legal Aspects|url=https://www.cryptomathic.com/news-events/blog/eidas-from-directive-to-regulation-legal-aspects|publisher=Cryptomathic|accessdate=18 March 2016}}</ref><ref name="EU-difference-regulation-directive">{{cite web|title=Regulations, Directives and other acts|url=http://europa.eu/eu-law/decision-making/legal-acts/index_en.htm|website=Europa.eu|publisher=The European Union|accessdate=18 March 2016|url-status=dead|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20131212034345/http://europa.eu/eu-law/decision-making/legal-acts/index_en.htm|archivedate=12 December 2013}}</ref>
